newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Deng's legacy to Hong Kong -- calm.
newsitem.headline: Deng's legacy to Hong Kong -- calm.

text.p: Deng Xiaoping's legacy to Hong Kong was reflected in the benign response to his death in the busy British colony which took the news in its stride.
Eulogies to Deng's leadership and his role as the architect of reform and reunification dominated the Hong Kong landscape on Friday.
Long lines of mourners formed outside the headquarters of the Xinhua News Agency, China's de facto diplomatic mission in Hong Kong.
Calm returned to the Hong Kong stock market following Thursday's dramatic surge and shares overcame profit-taking pressures to finish 33.52 points higher at 13,336.01.

Underpinned by a surging economy riding the crest of China's emergence as a boom market, financial worries have been relegated to the backburner as Hong Kong confronts the momentous changes in store when the it reverts to China in mid-1997.
Hong Kong's largest pro-Beijing party wrote to the family of China's late paramount leader on Friday requesting that some of his ashes be sent to the territory to mark the handover.
Deng died late on Wednesday at the age of 92 of complications from a lung infection and Parkinson's disease.

"We hope you can keep a part of Mr Deng's ashes until after Hong Kong's return to China in July 1997, to be scattered in the seas (here) in order to fulfil his last wish to come here himself after the return," wrote Tsang Yok-sing, chairman of the Democratic Alliance for the Betterment of Hong Kong.
Hong Kong, a British colony for more than 150 years, reverts to China at the stroke of midnight on Monday, June 30.
Deng's role in ordering the bloody military suppression of the democracy movement around Tiananmen in 1989, which ruptured Hong Kong's confidence in its future under Chinese rule, was not emphasised.

Senior members of Hong Kong's Democratic Party, which was born in the aftermath of the Tiananmen crackdown, paid their respects to Deng's memory, but were among the few voices to address the more controversial issues.
"We still talk about the disgrace of Mr Deng which very few people dare to speak about at this time," party vice-chairman Yeung Sam told reporters after tendering his condolences.
Deng's legacy to Hong Kong goes beyond the handover which ends what many Chinese see as a shameful period of foreign exploitation of China.

His open door reforms of 1979 opened the floodgates at a time when Hong Kong's manufacturing sector was bursting at the seams and chafing from the shortage of space and workers in the British colony. Hong Kong-owned factories mushroomed in China.

As a result, manufacturing's contribution to Hong Kong gross domestic product declined to less than 10 percent by the end of 1994 from 23.7 percent in 1980, said Yiu-Kwan Fan, dean of the School of Business at Hong Kong Baptist University.

But trade-related services in Hong Kong boomed as raw and semi-finished materials poured through Hong Kong to China, and finished goods poured out. In 1996, some 90 percent of Hong Kong's re-exports of HK$1.19 trillion ($161 billion) involved China.
Hong Kong is now China's largest foreign investor, ahead of economic giants the United States and Japan.

By 1995, Hong Kong had contributed a cumulative total of US$20.19 billion in investment, more than 50 percent of the total. More than 100,000 joint ventures in China are funded with Hong Kong capital.

China's large and growing contribution to Hong Kong's domestic economy is difficult to gauge because the territory does not restrict capital flows, said George Leung, economic adviser at the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corp Ltd.
"PRC (People's Republic of China) investment in Hong Kong is estimated at US$20 billion by some sources," Leung said.
This Chinese investment is rising steadily.

"The economic reform programmes were only possible because of the political stability in China, because there were no upheavals except for four weeks in May and June 1989," said Dave O'Rear, regional economist at The Economist Conferences, a regular series of meetings on politics and economics organised by the London-based magazine.

"Deng's greatest contribution is that he kept a very stable and prosperous China going for a long enough period of time that the issue of (the handover of Hong Kong to China in) 1997 could be dealt with by a China not in turmoil," O'Rear added.
